prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current neural solvers for combinatorial optimization problems, specifically Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs), predominantly rely on Transformer-based architectures. While effective on small scales, these models suffer from the quadratic complexity of self-attention mechanisms, making them computationally expensive and difficult to scale to large real-world instances. Furthermore, existing constructive solvers tend to rely heavily on greedy decoding strategies, which limits solution diversity and often results in premature convergence to local optima. There is a need for a constructive framework that is computationally lightweight, scalable, and inherently capable of generating diverse, high-quality solutions without relying on heavy heuristic post-processing during inference.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can overcome the scalability and diversity limitations of Transformers by utilizing a **Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet)** as the foundational constructive policy. GFlowNets are theoretically well-suited for sampling diverse candidates proportional to their rewards but can suffer from over-exploration of low-quality regions.

We propose to mitigate this by introducing an **Adversarial Training** mechanism. By pairing the GFlowNet (Generator) with a Discriminator network, we aim to guide the generative process toward high-reward regions. The core intuition is that the Generator should learn to produce solutions that are structurally indistinguishable from those refined by local search heuristics, effectively "distilling" the intelligence of search algorithms into the constructive policy itself.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose an end-to-end framework consisting of three main conceptual components: a Generator, a Discriminator, and a Hybrid Decoding strategy.

### 1. The Generator (GFlowNet via GNN)
Instead of a Transformer, we will employ a lightweight Graph Neural Network (GNN).
*   **Input Sparsification:** To ensure scalability, we will preprocess the problem instance into a sparse graph, retaining only a fixed number of nearest neighbors for each node.
*   **Construction Policy:** The GNN will encode node and edge features to output a policy (a heatmap of transition probabilities). We will treat the solution construction as a sequential decision-making process where the GFlowNet samples transitions to build a complete route.
*   **Objective:** The Generator will be trained using a trajectory balance objective, designed to ensure the probability of generating a solution is proportional to its reward.

### 2. The Adversarial Discriminator
We will introduce a secondary network to act as a quality critic.
*   **Adversarial Setup:** The Discriminator will be trained to distinguish between "raw" solutions produced directly by the Generator and "refined" solutions that have undergone a generic local search (e.g., destruction and reconstruction).
*   **Feedback Signal:** The score output by the Discriminator will be integrated into the Generator's reward function. This provides a dense learning signal, encouraging the Generator to produce initial solutions that already possess the characteristics of locally optimized routes.

### 3. Hybrid Decoding Strategy
To leverage the diversity of GFlowNets without sacrificing solution quality, we will implement a hybrid inference mechanism.
*   **Logic:** At each step of the route construction, the model will decide probabilistically whether to sample from the distribution (Exploration) or select the highest-probability edge (Exploitation/Greedy).
*   **Purpose:** This mechanism prevents the "tail" of the distribution from leading the solver into poor regions while maintaining enough stochasticity to avoid the determinism of pure greedy search.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Scalability:** A constructive neural solver that avoids the quadratic complexity of Transformers, enabling efficient training and inference on large-scale problem instances.
*   **Theoretical Novelty:** A framework that successfully integrates GFlowNets with adversarial learning, providing a method to curb over-exploration while preserving the inherent diversity benefits of flow networks.
*   **Practical Utility:** An end-to-end solver that generates high-quality solutions directly, reducing the dependency on computationally expensive post-hoc search algorithms during deployment.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a rigorous experimental framework to evaluate the Adversarial Generative Flow Network (AGFN). The experiments were designed to test performance on the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) and the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) across various scales, ranging from 200 to 10,000 nodes.

*   **Hardware and Environment:** All experiments were conducted on a server equipped with an NVIDIA Tesla V100-32G GPU and an Intel Xeon Gold 6148 CPU.
*   **Datasets (Synthetic):**
    *   We generated random instances where customer and depot coordinates were sampled from a unit square $[0, 1]^2$.
    *   **CVRP Details:** Customer demands were drawn from a uniform distribution $U[1, 9]$. Vehicle capacity was fixed at $C=50$ for all problem sizes.
    *   **Problem Sizes:** We generated test datasets for sizes $|V| \in \{200, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 5,000, 10,000\}$.
    *   **Test Set Volume:**
        *   For sizes 200, 500, 1,000, 2,000, and 3,000: 128 instances each.
        *   For sizes 5,000 and 10,000: 64 instances each.
*   **Datasets (Real-World Benchmarks):**
    *   **CVRPLib:** Used for cross-distribution generalization testing.
    *   **TSPLib:** Used for cross-distribution generalization testing.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Obj.:** Average total travel distance (objective value).
    *   **Gap (%):** The percentage gap relative to a baseline (often LKH-3 with 100 iterations or known optimal solutions).
    *   **Time (s):** Average wall-clock time required to solve a single instance.
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Heuristics:** LKH-3 (Lin-Kernighan-Helsgaun) at 100, 1,000, and 10,000 iterations; ACO (Ant Colony Optimization).
    *   **Neural Constructive:** POMO (Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima) and POMO (*8), GANCO (Generative Adversarial Network for Combinatorial Optimization).
    *   **Neural Improvement/Other:** NeuOpt, GFACS (GFlowNet with Ant Colony Sampling).
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Sparsification:** We constrained the graph such that each node retained only $k = |\nu|/4$ of its shortest outgoing edges.
    *   **Training Configuration:** We utilized sampling decoding (without greedy selection) during training. The number of sampled routes per instance ($\mathcal{N}$) was set to 20. The training round ratio between the generator and discriminator was $4:1$.
    *   **Inference Configuration:** We employed a hybrid decoding strategy. $\mathcal{N}$ was set to 100. The probability hyperparameter $\mathcal{P}$ (for sampling vs. greedy selection) was set to 0.05. No local search was applied to AGFN outputs during inference.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Ablation Study on Hybrid Decoding Strategy:**
*   We compared three decoding strategies: pure sampling, pure greedy, and our proposed hybrid decoding.
*   Pure sampling consistently resulted in the highest gap percentages across all tested CVRP and TSP sizes.
*   Pure greedy selection outperformed pure sampling but yielded higher gaps than the hybrid approach.
*   The hybrid decoding strategy consistently achieved the lowest performance gaps across CVRP200, CVRP500, CVRP1000, TSP200, TSP500, and TSP1000.
*   In specific cases such as CVRP1000 and TSP1000, the hybrid method significantly reduced the performance gap compared to both greedy and sampling baselines, confirming its effectiveness on larger-scale instances.

**Ablation Study on Discriminator Training:**
*   We investigated the impact of the method used to generate "true" samples for the discriminator (using our local search vs. LKH heuristic) and the impact of removing the adversarial component entirely.
*   The choice of search method (Internal Local Search vs. LKH) in the discriminator had negligible impact on performance; both methods led to similar convergence behaviors.
*   Incorporating the adversarial component significantly accelerated the convergence of the training curve compared to the non-adversarial setting.
*   The adversarial model achieved a superior (lower) average objective value compared to the non-adversarial model, which plateaued at a higher objective value.

**Performance and Generalization Observations:**
*   AGFN demonstrated strong scalability. While trained on 100-node instances, it successfully solved 5,000 and 10,000-node instances where baselines like LKH-3 failed to produce results due to computational constraints.
*   AGFN-100 significantly outperformed POMO and GFACS on real-world benchmark datasets (TSPLib and CVRPLib) in both objective quality and computation time.
*   AGFN consistently exhibited lower inference times compared to baselines like GFACS, NeuOpt, and GANCO, particularly as problem sizes increased to 1,000 nodes.
*   For very large instances (10,000 nodes), AGFN maintained an inference time of approximately 14.60 seconds.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex

\begin{center}
%\framebox[4.0in]{$\;$}
\fbox{\rule[-.5cm]{0cm}{4cm} \rule[-.5cm]{4cm}{0cm}}
\end{center}

\end{figure}
```

### Example Code for Tables

```latex
\label{sample-table}

\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The domain of Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) for Vehicle Routing Problems (VRPs) is currently dominated by construction-based solvers utilizing Transformer architectures. While effective on small-scale instances, these models face two critical limitations. First, the self-attention mechanism inherent to Transformers imposes a quadratic computational complexity, creating significant scalability bottlenecks when processing large-scale graphs. Second, standard constructive solvers often struggle to produce diverse solutions, leading to convergence on local optima due to a bias toward high-probability edges during greedy decoding. Existing alternatives, such as improvement-based methods or recent applications of Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets), either suffer from excessive inference times or rely heavily on external heuristics (e.g., Ant Colony Optimization) to guide exploration, thereby failing to function as efficient, standalone end-to-end constructive solvers. We require a framework that balances the diversity of probabilistic sampling with the quality of targeted construction without incurring the computational costs of Transformers.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose the development of an **Adversarial Generative Flow Network (AGFN)**, a novel framework that replaces the Transformer architecture with a lightweight Graph Neural Network (GNN) driven by GFlowNet principles.

Our core hypothesis is that we can train a GFlowNet generator to construct diverse, high-quality routes by coupling it with a **Discriminator network** in an adversarial setting. By training the Discriminator to distinguish between raw generated solutions and those refined by a local search operator, we can provide a nuanced scoring signal that augments the GFlowNet reward function. This adversarial feedback loop will guide the generator toward global optima more effectively than varying path length alone. Furthermore, we hypothesize that a **Hybrid Decoding** strategy—interleaving probabilistic sampling with greedy selection—will allow the model to generalize to problem sizes significantly larger than those seen during training.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Instance Representation and Sparsification
To ensure scalability, we will not operate on fully connected graphs. For a VRP instance represented by graph $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$, where $\mathcal{V}$ contains node features (coordinates) and $\mathcal{E}$ contains edge costs, we will construct a sparse graph $\mathcal{G}^*$. Each node will retain only its $k$ shortest outgoing edges (nearest neighbors).
We will define the input features by linearly projecting node coordinates $\mathbf{x}_v$ and edge distances $\mathbf{x}_e$ into high-dimensional vectors $\mathbf{h}_i^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{\bar{d}}$ and $\mathbf{e}_{ij}^0 \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

### 2. Generator Architecture (GNN-based GFlowNet)
Instead of a Transformer, we will design a specialized GNN to compute edge selection probabilities (heatmaps). The GNN will update node features $\mathbf{h}_i$ and edge features $\mathbf{e}_{ij}$ iteratively. For layer $l$, the update rule will be:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \mathbf { h } _ { i } ^ { l + 1 } = \mathbf { h } _ { i } ^ { l } + \mathrm { A C T } ( \mathrm { B N } ( \mathbf { U } ^ { l } \mathbf { h } _ { i } ^ { l } + \mathcal { A } _ { j \in \mathcal { N } _ { i } } ( \sigma ( \mathbf { e } _ { i j } ^ { l } ) \odot \mathbf { V } ^ { l } \mathbf { h } _ { j } ^ { l } ) ) ) , } \\ & { \mathbf { e } _ { i j } ^ { l + 1 } = \mathbf { e } _ { i j } ^ { l } + \mathrm { A C T } ( \mathrm { B N } ( \mathbf { P } ^ { l } \mathbf { e } _ { i j } ^ { l } + \mathbf { Q } ^ { l } \mathbf { h } _ { i } ^ { l } + \mathbf { R } ^ { l } \mathbf { h } _ { j } ^ { l } ) ) . } \end{array}
$$

Where:
*   $\mathbf{U}^l, \mathbf{V}^l, \mathbf{P}^l, \mathbf{Q}^l, \mathbf{R}^l$ are trainable weight matrices.
*   $\mathcal{A}$ is the aggregation function (mean pooling).
*   $\sigma$ is the sigmoid function and $\odot$ is the Hadamard product.
*   $\mathrm{ACT}$ is the SiLU activation function.

The final output will be passed through an MLP to produce a heatmap $\eta(\mathcal{G}^*, \pmb{\theta}_{generator})$ representing the edge probability distribution.

### 3. Adversarial Training Framework
The system will operate as a closed loop between a **Generator** and a **Discriminator**.

#### The Discriminator
The discriminator will evaluate complete paths. It receives two sets of inputs:
1.  $\mathcal{T}_{false}$: Original paths generated by the GFlowNet.
2.  $\mathcal{T}_{true}$: Paths enhanced via a generic local search (iterative destruction/reconstruction).

The discriminator outputs a score $\mathcal{S}(\tau) \in [0, 1]$. We will train it to assign scores close to 1 for enhanced paths and 0 for raw paths using the following loss:
$$ \mathcal { L } ( T ; \theta _ { d i s c r i m i n a t o r } ) = \frac { 1 } { M + N } ( \sum _ { \tau _ { m } \in \mathcal { T } _ { t r u e } } ( 1 - \mathcal { S } ( \tau _ { m } ) ) ^ { 2 } + \sum _ { \tau _ { n } \in \mathcal { T } _ { f a l s e } } \mathcal { S } ( \tau _ { n } ) ^ { 2 } ) . $$

#### The Generator (Reward Shaping and Loss)
The GFlowNet generator aims to construct trajectories $\tau = (s_0 \to s_1 \dots \to s_n)$. We will shape the reward $\widetilde{R}(\tau_k)$ by combining the negative path length (traditional objective) with the discriminator's quality score $S(\tau_k)$. This guides the model to favor solutions that "look" like locally optimized solutions. The reward formulation is:

$$ - \log \widetilde { R } ( \tau _ { k } ) = ( 1 - S ( \tau _ { k } ) ) + R ( \tau _ { k } ) - \frac { 1 } { K } \sum _ { t = 1 } ^ { K } R ( \tau _ { t } ) , $$

where $R(\tau_t)$ is the total length of path $\tau_t$.

To train the Generator, we will employ the **Trajectory Balance (TB)** objective, which enforces consistency between the forward policy $P_F$ and backward policy $P_B$:

$$ \mathcal { L } _ { T B } ( \mathcal { T } ; \theta _ { g e n e r a t o r } ) = \frac { 1 } { K } \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \left( \log \frac { Z _ { \theta } * P _ { F } ( \tau _ { k } ; \theta _ { g e n e r a t o r } ) } { \widetilde { R } ( \tau _ { k } ) * P _ { B } ( \tau _ { k } ; \theta _ { g e n e r a t o r } ) } \right) ^ { 2 } . $$

Here, $Z_\theta$ is the learnable partition function (total flow), and $P_F$ is the product of transition probabilities along the path derived from the GNN heatmap.

### 4. Hybrid Decoding Strategy
To balance exploration and exploitation during inference, we will implement a hybrid decoding mechanism. At each step $t$, the next node $s_{t+1}$ is selected based on a hyperparameter probability $\mathcal{P}$:

$$ s _ { t + 1 } = { \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { s , } & { { \mathrm { w i t h ~ p r o b a b i l i t y ~ } } \mathcal { P } } \\ { s ^ { * } , } & { { \mathrm { w i t h ~ p r o b a b i l i t y ~ } } 1 - \mathcal { P } } \end{array} \right. } $$

where $s$ is sampled from the distribution $P_F(s_{t+1}|s_t)$ (exploration), and $s^*$ is the argmax of that distribution (greedy exploitation). This ensures the model effectively searches the solution space without converging prematurely to suboptimal regions.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Structural Efficiency:** By replacing Transformers with a sparse GNN, we expect to achieve linear complexity relative to problem size, enabling the solver to train on and solve significantly larger instances than current SOTA constructive neural solvers.
2.  **Generative Quality via Adversarial Learning:** The integration of the Discriminator provides a denser, more informative learning signal than simple path length, allowing the GFlowNet to learn features of high-quality solutions that are typically only found via local search.
3.  **End-to-End Constructive Capability:** Unlike recent "improvement-based" neural solvers, AGFN will generate high-quality solutions in a single constructive pass (using hybrid decoding), removing the dependency on time-consuming post-hoc heuristic search algorithms during inference.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
